name: perforating folliculitis
aliases: perforating folliculitis of Mehregan and Coskey

clinicalPearls: A perforating dermatosis in which the perforation is centred on a hair follicle, presenting as discrete follicular keratotic papules, each often containing a curled or fragmented hair within a central plug.
Favours the hair-bearing extensor surfaces of the limbs, buttocks and trunk, and is frequently pruritic.
Regarded as part of the acquired perforating dermatosis spectrum and, like the others, associated with chronic kidney disease, haemodialysis and diabetes mellitus.

Histology shows a dilated follicular infundibulum plugged with keratin, degenerate collagen and inflammatory debris, with a perforation through the follicular wall through which material is eliminated.
A curled hair shaft is often trapped within the follicular plug and may act as the initiating foreign body driving the perforation.
Differentiation from Kyrle disease and reactive perforating collagenosis rests on the follicular localisation of the perforating channel.
Management follows the acquired perforating dermatosis approach: emollients, topical retinoids or corticosteroids, keratolytics, phototherapy and control of the underlying systemic disorder.
Koebnerisation from scratching contributes to lesion development, so breaking the itch-scratch cycle is an important therapeutic goal.
reference.pathophysiology: Perforating folliculitis arises from injury to the follicular infundibulum, where retained keratin, a coiled or fractured hair shaft, and degenerate dermal connective tissue accumulate and are eliminated through a defect in the follicular wall. Follicular rupture provokes a foreign-body inflammatory response that facilitates transepithelial elimination of collagen and keratinous debris. In acquired cases the metabolic milieu of uraemia and diabetes, dermal microangiopathy, and repetitive scratch-induced trauma with Koebnerisation are considered key triggers, injuring the follicular epithelium and perpetuating the perforating process.
additionalInvestigations: skin biopsy demonstrating the plugged follicle with perforation of the follicular wall and eliminated debris
renal function tests and estimated glomerular filtration rate
swab of pustular lesions to exclude infective folliculitis where clinically suspected
redFlags: presentation without known renal or metabolic disease, warranting systemic screening
pustular or tender lesions suggesting superimposed infective folliculitis requiring microbiological assessment
widespread refractory disease indicating poorly controlled uraemia or diabetes
signs of secondary bacterial infection from excoriation
reference.prognosis: The condition tends to be chronic and relapsing, with individual follicular papules resolving over weeks while new lesions continue to appear; improvement generally follows better control of the underlying systemic disease and reduction of scratching.
pitfalls: misdiagnosing pruritic follicular papules as ordinary keratosis pilaris or infective folliculitis and missing the perforating pathology
not sectioning the biopsy through the follicle, so the follicular perforation is not visualised
overlooking associated chronic kidney disease or diabetes
relying on antibacterial therapy alone when the process is a non-infective perforating dermatosis
management: Optimise control of the underlying chronic kidney disease and diabetes mellitus that drive the eruption
Control pruritus and interrupt the itch-scratch cycle with emollients, topical corticosteroids and antihistamines
Use keratolytics and topical retinoids to address the follicular hyperkeratosis
Consider narrowband ultraviolet B phototherapy for widespread or refractory pruritic disease
Consider oral retinoids or allopurinol in resistant cases
Treat secondary infection of excoriated lesions where present
Refer to dermatology and liaise with nephrology in dialysis patients
